questions.question: Which statement best distinguishes inflammation from infection?
choices: Inflammation always proves bacterial invasion
Infection is microbial invasion, whereas inflammation is a host response that can also follow sterile injury
Inflammation occurs only when fever is present
Infection never causes inflammation
questions.explanation: Infection is one trigger for inflammation, but trauma, ischemia, allergy, autoimmune disease, crystals, burns, and toxins can produce sterile inflammatory responses. Cause requires clinical evaluation.

questions.question: Which vascular changes most directly produce warmth and swelling during acute inflammation?
choices: Vasodilation and increased vascular permeability
Persistent vasoconstriction and reduced protein movement
Decreased local blood flow and complete endothelial closure
Reduced mediator release and lymphocyte destruction
questions.explanation: Vasodilation increases local blood flow and warmth, while increased permeability allows protein-rich fluid to enter tissue and create edema. Pain and impaired function arise from mediators and tissue effects.

questions.question: Which leukocyte is commonly prominent early in acute bacterial inflammation?
choices: Neutrophil
Erythrocyte
Platelet
Fibroblast
questions.explanation: Neutrophils are rapidly recruited to many acute bacterial inflammatory sites and phagocytose microbes and debris. The entire differential and clinical context remain necessary for interpretation.

questions.question: Which pattern is most characteristic of chronic inflammation?
choices: Only transient vasodilation with complete resolution in minutes
Macrophages and lymphocytes with simultaneous tissue injury, repair and fibrosis
Absence of cytokines and tissue damage
Platelet activation without leukocyte involvement
questions.explanation: Persistent triggers recruit macrophages, lymphocytes, and plasma cells. Ongoing mediator release can produce tissue destruction while angiogenesis, fibroblast activity, and fibrosis occur at the same time.

questions.question: Why does a client often feel cold and shiver while a fever is rising?
choices: The hypothalamic set point has risen, so the current temperature is perceived as too low
The temperature set point has fallen below normal
Sweating has already removed all body heat
Fever and hyperthermia use identical mechanisms
questions.explanation: Pyrogen-driven prostaglandin signaling raises the hypothalamic set point. Vasoconstriction, chills, and shivering generate and conserve heat until body temperature approaches the new target.

questions.question: Which finding favors dangerous hyperthermia rather than a routine regulated fever?
choices: Chills as a cytokine-mediated set point rises
Severe heat exposure with hot skin, altered mental status and very high temperature
Mild postoperative temperature elevation without symptoms
Sweating as a fever resolves
questions.explanation: Hyperthermia results when heat production or exposure exceeds heat loss without a higher regulated set point. Heat exposure plus neurologic change requires immediate cooling and emergency response.

questions.question: How should the RN interpret a declining C-reactive protein after treatment?
choices: It proves that a specific bacterial pathogen is eradicated
It may support decreasing inflammatory activity but must be interpreted with symptoms, examination and other trends
It guarantees tissue repair is complete
It rules out every infection
questions.explanation: C-reactive protein is a nonspecific inflammatory marker. A falling trend can support improvement, but it neither identifies the cause nor replaces assessment, cultures, imaging, and functional outcomes.

questions.question: During which overlapping wound-healing phase do angiogenesis, fibroblast activity, granulation tissue and re-epithelialization predominate?
choices: Hemostasis
Proliferation
Initial vasoconstriction only
Necrosis
questions.explanation: The proliferative phase builds new vascular and connective tissue, deposits collagen, contracts the wound, and restores the epithelial surface. It overlaps with inflammation and later remodeling.

questions.question: Which modifiable factors should the RN address to support wound healing?
choices: Tobacco exposure, poor nutrition, uncontrolled glucose, pressure and inadequate perfusion
Age and genetic history only
Scar color only
Room number and meal preference
questions.explanation: Tobacco exposure, nutritional deficits, hyperglycemia, pressure, moisture and impaired perfusion can delay repair. Nursing care targets these risks while following the prescribed wound plan.

questions.question: A postoperative client has increasing incisional pain, tachypnea, new confusion, hypotension and falling urine output. What is the priority action?
choices: Document expected inflammation and reassess tomorrow
Assess ABCs and perfusion and activate the appropriate urgent or sepsis response pathway
Apply a warm compress and finish routine rounds
Wait for marked redness before reporting
questions.explanation: The systemic cluster suggests organ dysfunction rather than an expected local healing response. Immediate assessment, stabilization, escalation, and protocol-based action take priority over routine wound care.
